title: Credit Reports
description: Read the file behind the score, fix what is wrong, and lock what you can.
wolfLine: The report is the story. Read it before someone else does.

credit-report.definition: The file of your credit accounts: what you owe, whether you paid on time, and who has looked. The score is a number built from this file.
credit-report.example: A report lists a $420 card balance and a car loan. It does not, by itself, show the score.

credit-bureau.definition: A company that collects credit information and sells reports. The three big ones are Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
credit-bureau.example: A loan might show on Experian and not yet on Equifax.

credit-freeze.definition: A lock you place at each bureau so new lenders cannot pull your report. You lift it when you want to apply.
credit-freeze.example: Freeze all three, then thaw one the week you shop for a car loan.

lessons.title: Report and Score
lessons.summary: The report is the story. The score is one number squeezed out of it.

steps.context: A [[credit report]] lists your accounts and whether you paid. A [[credit score]] is a number built from that file. The free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com do not include the score.
steps.prompt: What is a credit report?
choices: The file of your accounts, payments, and inquiries
steps.explain: The file comes first. The score is calculated from it.

steps.prompt: Your credit report and your credit score are the same thing.
steps.explain: One is the file. The other is a number made from the file.

steps.prompt: Where do the free weekly reports come from, with no score attached?
steps.explain: That is the official site. As of 2026 the three bureaus still offer those reports weekly.

steps.prompt: Why read the report if you already know the score?
choices: The report shows the accounts and errors behind the number
The score already lists every account
steps.explain: You cannot fix a wrong account from a number alone.

steps.prompt: Match each word to what it is.
pairs: The file of accounts and payments
A number built from that file
A lender’s check when you apply

steps.prompt: A free credit report from AnnualCreditReport.com includes your FICO score.
steps.explain: The report is free. The score is a separate product.

lessons.title: Three Bureaus
lessons.summary: Equifax, Experian, TransUnion. None of them has to match the others.

steps.context: A [[credit bureau]] collects your credit data and sells reports. The three nationwide ones are Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. A lender might report to one and not the others, so the files can differ.
steps.prompt: How many big nationwide credit bureaus are there?
steps.explain: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.

steps.prompt: Match each bureau to the file it keeps.
pairs: Its own copy of your report
A third report that can differ

steps.prompt: If one bureau’s report is clean, the other two must be clean too.
steps.explain: Each file is its own. Check all three.

steps.prompt: Why check all three reports?
choices: An error or a fraud account may sit on only one of them
The law says you pick a favorite
They always show the same score
steps.explain: One clean file does not clear the other two.

steps.prompt: Who do you freeze if you want new lenders blocked?
choices: Each bureau, because a freeze at one does not cover the others
steps.explain: Three files, three locks.

steps.prompt: Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion are credit ___.
steps.explain: They keep the reports.

lessons.title: Free Reports
lessons.summary: Once a week, from the official site. Still true in 2026.

steps.title: Where the free ones live
steps.body:
AnnualCreditReport.com is the official site for the free reports required by federal law. Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion made weekly free reports permanent in 2023, and that was still the offer in 2026.

Other sites may sell you a score, a subscription, or nothing. The weekly reports do not include your credit score.

steps.prompt: How often could you get a free report from each big bureau in 2026?
steps.explain: Weekly, at the official site.

steps.prompt: Which site is the official one?
choices: Any site that says “free score” in an ad
A link in a random text
steps.explain: Type it yourself. Do not trust a look-alike.

steps.prompt: The free weekly report includes your credit score.
steps.explain: It is the report, not the score.

steps.prompt: A site asks for a credit card “to verify you” before showing a free report. What do you do?
choices: Leave. The official weekly reports do not require a card
Send a photo of your license in a text
steps.explain: Paying is the clue that it is not the official free report.

steps.prompt: You want all three files. What do you request?
choices: A report from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion
steps.explain: Three files. One sitting can still hide a problem.

lessons.title: Reading a Report
lessons.summary: Names, balances, and a line that should not be there.

steps.context: Read a report line by line: who you owe, how much, and whether a late payment is listed.

steps.prompt: Which line needs a harder look?
choices: QuickCash Collections, an account you never opened
The car loan you know about
steps.explain: Unknown accounts are how fraud hides.

steps.prompt: A balance on the report means you should pay it today, even if you do not recognize the account.
steps.explain: Recognize it first. An account that is not yours gets disputed, not paid on a hunch.

lessons.title: An Account That Is Not Yours
lessons.summary: Tap the line that does not belong.

steps.context: Fraud often shows up as a new account you do not remember. That is the line to dispute.

doc.title: Your report · one bureau
doc.subtitle: You have never shopped at Luma

lines.label: Luma Store card · opened last month · balance

doc.note: The Luma card was opened last month. You did not apply.

steps.prompt: Which line is the account you never opened?
steps.explain: Luma Store card, opened last month, is not yours. The others match accounts you know.

steps.prompt: What do you do about the Luma card?
choices: Dispute it with the bureau, and tell the lender it is fraud
Pay the $890 so it goes away
Ignore it. Strange accounts fall off in a week
steps.explain: Paying a fraud account can look like you accept it.

steps.prompt: If the fake $890 were counted, how much would it add to the $180 and $2,100 you really owe?
steps.explain: It adds its own $890. $180 + $2,100 + $890 = $3,170, but $890 of that is not yours.

steps.prompt: An account you never opened can still hurt your score while it sits on the report.
steps.explain: The score reads the file, including the bad lines.

steps.prompt: You see the same fake account on only one bureau. Do you still act?
choices: Yes. Fix the file that has it, and check the other two
No. One out of three is fine
Only if the balance is over $10,000
steps.explain: Lenders read the file they happen to pull.

steps.prompt: Put a fraud response in order.
items: Confirm the account is not yours
Dispute it with the bureau and the lender
steps.explain: Name it, challenge it, lock new applications, then look again.

lessons.title: Disputing an Error
lessons.summary: Tell the bureau what is wrong, in writing, and keep a copy.

steps.context: If a report is wrong, you dispute it: you tell the [[credit bureau]] what is incorrect and ask for a fix. Do it with each bureau that shows the error. Send copies of proof, and keep your own copy. This is not the same as asking your bank to reverse a charge.
steps.prompt: An old address and a paid-off loan still show as open. What is that?
choices: Facts you are not allowed to question
steps.explain: Wrong facts get challenged.

steps.prompt: Put a dispute in order.
items: Find the wrong line on the report
Write what is wrong and include proof
Send it to the bureau that shows it
Read the result and check the report again
steps.explain: Find it, explain it, send it, confirm the fix.

steps.prompt: You should dispute a wrong account with every bureau that lists it.
steps.explain: A fix at one bureau does not rewrite the others.

steps.prompt: What belongs in the dispute?
choices: What is wrong, and a copy of anything that proves it
Only your opinion, with no details
Your card number in a text to a stranger
steps.explain: Specific and documented.

steps.prompt: The bureau corrects the fake account. What do you do next?
choices: Check that the line is actually gone, on a fresh report
steps.explain: Trust the new report, not the promise.

steps.prompt: Paying a collection you do not owe is the fastest way to clean a report.
steps.explain: Pay what you owe. Dispute what you do not.

lessons.title: Freezing Your Credit
lessons.summary: A lock on new loans. You still use the cards you already have.

steps.context: A [[credit freeze]] (also called a security freeze) stops new lenders from seeing your report. You place one at each [[credit bureau]], for free, and lift it when you want to apply. Cards you already have keep working.
steps.prompt: What does a credit freeze do?
choices: Stops new lenders from pulling your report until you lift it
steps.explain: It blocks new credit. It does not wipe history.

steps.prompt: A freeze at Experian also freezes Equifax and TransUnion.
steps.explain: Each bureau needs its own freeze.

steps.prompt: You want to apply for a car loan next week. What do you do with the freeze?
choices: Lift it, apply, then freeze again
Leave it and hope the dealer guesses
Close the loan you already have
steps.explain: Thaw, shop, lock.

steps.prompt: Does a freeze stop you from using a card you already have?
choices: Yes. Every card is frozen shut
steps.explain: The lock is on new applications.

steps.prompt: Placing a credit freeze is free by law.
steps.explain: You do not pay the bureau to freeze or to lift a freeze.

steps.prompt: When is a freeze especially worth it?
choices: After a data leak, or if a fake account just showed up
When you want a higher score this week
steps.explain: It does not raise the score. It makes the next fake account harder.

lessons.title: How Long Marks Stay
lessons.summary: Most bad news lasts years. The clock is federal, not a rumor.

steps.title: The usual clocks
steps.body:
Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, most negative marks stay about seven years. A late payment is in that group. A Chapter 7 bankruptcy can stay up to 10 years. A hard inquiry stays about two years.

These are the federal limits. Paying a collection does not rewind the clock to zero, and a credit freeze does not delete old marks.

steps.prompt: About how long can a late payment stay on a report?
steps.explain: Seven years is the usual federal limit for late payments.

steps.prompt: About how long can a Chapter 7 bankruptcy stay?
steps.explain: Chapter 7 is the long one: up to 10 years.

steps.prompt: About how long does a hard inquiry stay?
steps.explain: Two years, and the score often cares less after the first year.

steps.prompt: A credit freeze deletes late payments.
steps.explain: A freeze blocks new pulls. It does not erase history.

steps.prompt: A late payment is reported in 2026. About what year does that seven-year clock run out?
